passage: Monday: Tenzin handed over his maths test at the dinner table. His mother Binita read the mark and her voice rose, "How can you fail again? What have you been doing?" Tenzin went silent and stared at his rice. He felt very small. Tuesday: he didn't speak much at breakfast, and Binita's mouth was still tight. He decided to wait. Thursday: after tea, when the flat was calm and Binita was folding clothes, he said, "Mummy, I want to get better at maths. Can you help me make a plan?" She stopped folding. "Okay," she said in a softer voice. "Let's look at the mistakes together tonight." Tenzin nodded and fetched his pencil.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do while his mother shouted on Monday?
qa.a: He went silent and stared at his rice.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when his mother shouted about his mark?
qa.a: Very small, which is why he went quiet instead of answering back.

qa.q: Why was Thursday a better time for Tenzin to talk to his mother?
qa.a: Things had cooled, and the flat was calm, so Tenzin could say he wanted to improve and ask for help with a plan without a fight.

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when she shouted about the test?
qa.a: Probably worried and frustrated about his mark, though the shouting made Tenzin shrink; later she softened once he asked for her help.

grounding: A child goes quiet when a parent shouts about failing, waits for things to cool, then asks for help with a plan.
